questions.stem: A 24-year-old client had open reduction and internal fixation of a tibial fracture 10 hours ago and has a long-leg splint. The client rates pain 10 of 10 despite IV hydromorphone 30 minutes ago, and the pain gets worse when the nurse gently moves the toes. The toes are pale and cool, capillary refill is 4 seconds, and the client reports tingling over the top of the foot. A pedal pulse is weak but present. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Notify the surgeon immediately about the findings
Loosen the splint dressing and keep the leg at heart level
Elevate the leg on two pillows above the heart
Apply ice packs directly over the splint to reduce swelling
Give another dose of hydromorphone and reassess in 1 hour

parameters.text: Pain level, especially with passive movement
Sensation and movement of the toes
Oral temperature checked with each set of vital signs
Bowel sounds in four quadrants and passing of flatus
Fingerstick blood glucose before meals and at bedtime

rationale.correct: Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia, pallor; pulses fade late. Notify the surgeon, remove constriction and keep the limb at heart level.

perOption.c1: Pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia and pallor after a tibial fracture point to compartment syndrome; a pulse can still be present.
perOption.c2: DVT causes swelling and calf pain but not pain on passive toe movement with numbness this early.
perOption.c3: Fat embolism causes breathing problems, confusion and a petechial rash, not a local limb picture.
perOption.c4: Pain that does not respond to opioids and worsens with passive stretch is not expected.
perOption.a1: Compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency that may need fasciotomy within hours.
perOption.a2: Releasing pressure and keeping the limb at heart level (not elevated) supports blood flow.
perOption.a3: Elevation above the heart lowers arterial pressure and worsens compartment perfusion.
perOption.a4: Ice can further reduce blood flow in compartment syndrome.
perOption.a5: More opioid hides a worsening sign and delays emergency treatment.
perOption.p1: Rising pain is the earliest sign that pressure is increasing.
perOption.p2: Worsening numbness or weakness shows nerve damage is progressing.
perOption.p3: Fever is not a key sign of compartment syndrome.
perOption.p4: Bowel function is unrelated to this complication.
perOption.p5: Glucose does not reflect limb perfusion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Three hours after a cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery, a client reports new, severe lower back pain. The groin site is soft with no hematoma. Blood pressure has dropped from 132/80 to 96/58 mm Hg, and heart rate has risen from 78 to 112/min. What is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.text: A vasovagal reaction caused by pain from lying flat on the back for several hours
Retroperitoneal bleeding from the puncture in the femoral artery
A reaction to the contrast dye given during the procedure
Muscle strain from keeping the leg straight after the procedure

rationale.correct: Retroperitoneal bleeding after femoral access may show no groin hematoma; back or flank pain with signs of hypovolemia needs urgent reporting.

perOption.a: A vasovagal reaction causes a slow heart rate, not tachycardia.
perOption.b: Back or flank pain with falling blood pressure and rising heart rate, without a visible groin hematoma, suggests bleeding into the retroperitoneum.
perOption.c: Contrast reactions usually cause hives, itching or wheezing, and back pain is not typical.
perOption.d: Muscle strain does not cause hypotension and tachycardia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with alcohol-related cirrhosis, ascites and a history of variceal banding is scheduled for a percutaneous liver biopsy this morning to stage the disease. The nurse reviews the morning laboratory results. Which result should the nurse report to the provider before the procedure?

options.text: Serum albumin 2.9 g/dL
INR 2.1
Serum sodium 134 mEq/L
Total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Before a liver biopsy, check clotting studies and platelets; a prolonged INR or low platelets must be reported because the liver bleeds easily.

perOption.a: Low albumin is common in cirrhosis and does not by itself delay a biopsy.
perOption.b: A high INR raises the risk of bleeding from the liver, a highly vascular organ; the provider may give vitamin K or plasma or change the plan.
perOption.c: Mild hyponatremia is common in cirrhosis and does not affect biopsy safety.
perOption.d: Raised bilirubin reflects liver disease but does not change the bleeding risk of the procedure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after a thoracentesis that removed 1,200 mL of fluid from the right side, the client reports sudden sharp chest pain and shortness of breath. Respiratory rate is 30/min and SpO2 is 87%. Which additional finding would the nurse expect if a pneumothorax has developed?

options.text: Crackles heard over both lung bases with a productive cough
Breath sounds that are absent on the side of the procedure
Wheezing heard throughout both lungs on expiration
Dullness to percussion over the right lower chest

rationale.correct: After thoracentesis, sudden chest pain and dyspnea with absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side suggest pneumothorax.

perOption.a: Crackles suggest fluid in the alveoli, not air in the pleural space.
perOption.b: Air in the pleural space stops sound from reaching the chest wall on the affected side.
perOption.c: Wheezing reflects narrowed airways, such as in asthma.
perOption.d: Dullness suggests fluid or consolidation; a pneumothorax sounds hyperresonant.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic hernia repair at 0800. At 0630 the nurse completes the preoperative checklist. Which findings should the nurse report to the surgeon or anesthesia provider before the client goes to the operating room? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client took a dose of apixaban last evening
The client ate toast with coffee 2 hours ago
The consent form is signed and witnessed
A temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) and a new cough
The client took metoprolol with a sip of water this morning
The client's potassium is 4.1 mEq/L

rationale.correct: Report recent anticoagulant doses, a break in fasting, and signs of infection before surgery; continued beta-blockers, a complete consent and normal labs are expected.

perOption.a: Anticoagulants are usually stopped before surgery; a recent dose raises bleeding risk.
perOption.b: Eating solid food within the fasting window increases the risk of aspiration during anesthesia.
perOption.c: A complete consent is expected and does not need reporting.
perOption.d: Signs of infection may delay elective surgery.
perOption.e: Beta-blockers are usually continued before surgery as prescribed.
perOption.f: This is within the normal range.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client is on the first day after a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) with continuous bladder irrigation. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or should be reported to the provider.

rows.text: Light pink urine with a few small clots
Bright red urine with thick clots and output less than the irrigation going in
Bladder spasms when the client feels the urge to urinate
New confusion with a serum sodium of 126 mEq/L

rationale.correct: After TURP, pink urine, small clots and spasms are expected; bright red bleeding, blocked outflow and hyponatremia with confusion must be reported.

perOption.r1:c1: Light pink drainage with small clots is expected after TURP.
perOption.r1:c2: This is the expected color on day 1.
perOption.r2:c1: Bright red drainage with clots and low output suggests bleeding and a blocked catheter.
perOption.r2:c2: Arterial bleeding and possible obstruction need prompt attention.
perOption.r3:c1: Bladder spasms are common with a large catheter after TURP and are treated with prescribed antispasmodics.
perOption.r3:c2: Spasms are expected and usually managed with medication.
perOption.r4:c1: Confusion and hyponatremia suggest absorption of irrigating fluid (TURP syndrome).
perOption.r4:c2: Low sodium with confusion is a serious complication.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis has just had a paracentesis that removed 5 L of ascitic fluid. Thirty minutes later, blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg (before the procedure, 124/76), heart rate is 116/min and the client feels dizzy. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed and notify the provider about the low blood pressure
Measure the abdominal girth and compare it with the girth before the procedure
Send the ascitic fluid sample to the lab and check the puncture site for leaking
Encourage the client to drink 500 mL of water to replace the lost volume

rationale.correct: Large-volume paracentesis can cause hypotension from fluid shifts; position the client, report, and expect albumin replacement.

perOption.a: Removing a large volume can shift fluid out of the blood vessels and cause hypotension; positioning and prompt reporting come first, and albumin may be ordered.
perOption.b: Girth shows how much fluid was removed but does not treat the hypotension.
perOption.c: These are routine tasks after the client is stable.
perOption.d: Oral water does not quickly restore blood volume and may worsen low sodium.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: On the first day after an open abdominal surgery, a client has a temperature of 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), diminished breath sounds at both bases and an SpO2 of 93% on room air. The client has been reluctant to use the incentive spirometer because of incisional pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic, then coach incentive spirometer use 10 times an hour
Ask the provider for a prescription for an antibiotic to treat a wound infection
Restrict oral and IV fluids to 1 L a day to reduce the risk of fluid in the lungs
Keep the client in bed with the head of the bed flat to reduce incisional pain

rationale.correct: Atelectasis is common early after surgery; treat pain, then use incentive spirometry, deep breathing, coughing and early walking.

perOption.a: Low-grade fever and reduced breath sounds early after surgery suggest atelectasis; pain control makes deep breathing possible.
perOption.b: Wound infections usually appear 3 to 5 days after surgery, not on day 1.
perOption.c: Fluid restriction would thicken secretions and is not indicated.
perOption.d: Lying flat and staying in bed worsen atelectasis.

questions.stem: A client had coronary artery bypass surgery 6 hours ago. Over the last hour, mediastinal chest tube drainage has dropped suddenly from 150 mL/hr to 10 mL/hr. Blood pressure is 82/64 mm Hg (pulse pressure 18), heart rate 128/min, central venous pressure 18 mm Hg (it was 8), the neck veins are distended and the heart sounds are muffled. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Notify the surgeon immediately and prepare for emergency sternal reopening or pericardiocentesis
Check the mediastinal chest tubes for kinks or clots
Give furosemide IV to lower the high central venous pressure
Place the client flat with the legs raised and wait for the blood pressure to improve
Increase the suction on the chest tube drainage system to the highest setting

rationale.correct: Tamponade after cardiac surgery: sudden drop in chest tube drainage, hypotension, narrow pulse pressure, high CVP, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. Notify the surgeon at once.

perOption.c1: Sudden drop in drainage, hypotension with a narrow pulse pressure, rising CVP, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds point to tamponade.
perOption.c2: Bleeding causes low, not high, CVP and flat neck veins.
perOption.c3: Tension pneumothorax causes tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds; muffled heart sounds and stopped drainage point to tamponade.
perOption.c4: MI can cause hypotension, but sudden loss of chest tube drainage with high CVP fits tamponade.
perOption.a1: Tamponade needs urgent removal of the blood compressing the heart.
perOption.a2: A blocked tube can cause blood to collect around the heart; restoring flow per policy may help.
perOption.a3: Diuresis lowers preload, which the compressed heart depends on, and worsens hypotension.
perOption.a4: Waiting delays the definitive treatment the client needs.
perOption.a5: Changing suction beyond the prescribed level is not a safe or effective treatment for tamponade.
perOption.p1: A narrow pulse pressure and falling blood pressure show worsening compression.
perOption.p2: A rising CVP reflects blood backing up as the heart cannot fill.
perOption.p3: Specific gravity does not guide emergency treatment of tamponade.
perOption.p4: Glucose control matters after surgery but does not track tamponade.
perOption.p5: Temperature is routine and not specific to tamponade.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with COPD received IV morphine for pain 2 hours ago and is now drowsy. Arterial blood gases: pH 7.28, PaCO2 62 mm Hg, HCO3 27 mEq/L, PaO2 58 mm Hg. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The client's blood gases show {{b1}}, which is {{b2}}, most likely because of {{b3}}.

options.text: respiratory acidosis
metabolic acidosis
respiratory alkalosis
uncompensated
fully compensated
partly compensated by the lungs
hypoventilation from the opioid
vomiting and loss of stomach acid
anxiety and rapid breathing

rationale.correct: pH below 7.35 with a PaCO2 above 45 and a normal HCO3 is uncompensated respiratory acidosis; opioid hypoventilation is a common cause in COPD.

perOption.b1:a: Low pH with a high PaCO2 is respiratory acidosis.
perOption.b1:b: Metabolic acidosis would have a low HCO3.
perOption.b1:c: Alkalosis would have a high pH and low PaCO2.
perOption.b2:a: HCO3 is at the top of normal, so the kidneys have not yet compensated.
perOption.b2:b: Full compensation would bring the pH back into the normal range.
perOption.b2:c: The lungs are the cause here; they cannot compensate for their own problem.
perOption.b3:a: Opioids depress breathing, and CO2 builds up quickly in a client with COPD.
perOption.b3:c: Rapid breathing lowers CO2 and causes alkalosis.

questions.stem: A client with a traumatic brain injury has been stable for 12 hours. The nurse now finds the client harder to arouse, with the right pupil larger than the left and sluggish. Which set of vital signs would most strongly suggest the intracranial pressure is rising toward herniation?

options.text: BP 92/50 mm Hg, heart rate 128/min, respirations 28/min, shallow and labored
BP 188/62 mm Hg, heart rate 48/min, respirations irregular with pauses
BP 146/88 mm Hg, heart rate 96/min, respirations 20/min and regular
BP 110/72 mm Hg, heart rate 62/min, respirations 14/min and regular

rationale.correct: Cushing's triad (high systolic pressure with a wide pulse pressure, slow pulse and irregular breathing) is a late sign of rising ICP and needs emergency action.

perOption.a: Low blood pressure with a fast heart rate suggests shock, not rising intracranial pressure.
perOption.b: Cushing's triad (widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing) is a late sign of rising ICP and impending herniation.
perOption.c: These are mildly raised but do not show the pattern of brainstem compression.
perOption.d: These are normal and do not suggest herniation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for 2 years for rheumatoid arthritis stopped it 4 days ago when the prescription ran out. The client now has severe weakness, vomiting and abdominal pain. Blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg, sodium 126 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L and glucose 58 mg/dL. Which prescription should the nurse expect to give first?

options.text: Oral prednisone 20 mg, restarting the client's usual home dose
IV hydrocortisone and rapid infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride with dextrose
IV regular insulin and dextrose to bring down the high serum potassium
IV furosemide to remove the extra potassium and fluid through the kidneys quickly

rationale.correct: Stopping long-term steroids suddenly can cause adrenal crisis: hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia. Treat with IV hydrocortisone and IV saline with dextrose.

perOption.a: The client is vomiting and in shock; oral steroids will not act fast enough.
perOption.b: These findings are adrenal crisis from stopping long-term steroids; IV hydrocortisone and fluid with glucose are life-saving.
perOption.c: The high potassium is from cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; it improves with hydrocortisone and fluids, and insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.
perOption.d: The client is volume depleted; a diuretic would worsen shock.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client in status epilepticus has a prescription for a loading dose of IV phenytoin. The client's IV line has 5% dextrose in water infusing. What should the nurse do before giving the phenytoin?

options.text: Give the phenytoin dose through the same line by IV push over 1 minute
Flush the line with 0.9% sodium chloride before and after the dose
Mix the phenytoin into the bag of 5% dextrose and run it over 2 hours
Give the phenytoin intramuscularly instead to avoid the dextrose problem

rationale.correct: Phenytoin is given IV only with normal saline, slowly (50 mg/min or less in adults), with cardiac and blood pressure monitoring.

perOption.a: Phenytoin given quickly can cause hypotension and dysrhythmias, and it precipitates with dextrose.
perOption.b: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose; it is given in saline at no more than 50 mg/min with cardiac monitoring.
perOption.c: Phenytoin forms crystals in dextrose solutions.
perOption.d: IM phenytoin is erratically absorbed and damages tissue.

questions.stem: Review the 1600 findings. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

segments.text: Pain is 4 of 10 at the incision
450 mL of bright red blood in 2 hours
Pedal pulses are present on both feet

rationale.correct: Restlessness, thirst, high drain output, falling blood pressure, rising heart rate and low urine output show hemorrhage with hypoperfusion.

perOption.s2: Restlessness and thirst are early signs of reduced brain perfusion and fluid loss.
perOption.s4: Moderate pain is expected after hip replacement.
perOption.s6: Drain output this high shows active bleeding.
perOption.s8: Blood pressure has dropped steadily since surgery.
perOption.s10: Rising heart rate is compensation for blood loss.
perOption.s12: Present pulses show the limb is perfused.
perOption.s14: Less than 30 mL/hr shows the kidneys are poorly perfused.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}} caused by {{b2}}.

options.text: hypovolemic shock
septic shock
cardiogenic shock
surgical bleeding
a reaction to the anesthetic
a pulmonary embolism

rationale.correct: Hemorrhage after hip replacement presents as hypovolemic shock: hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria and a falling hemoglobin.

perOption.b1:a: Falling blood pressure, tachycardia, low urine output and a large drop in hemoglobin show hypovolemic shock.
perOption.b1:b: There is no fever or infection source this soon after surgery.
perOption.b1:c: Nothing points to heart failure; the loss of blood explains the picture.
perOption.b2:a: Bright red drain output and a hemoglobin drop from 12.4 to 7.6 g/dL show bleeding from the surgical site.
perOption.b2:b: Anesthetic effects would not cause ongoing blood loss and falling hemoglobin.
perOption.b2:c: PE can cause hypotension, but the drain output and hemoglobin drop point to bleeding.

questions.stem: Which complication is the client at greatest risk for developing in the next hour?

options.text: Dislocation of the hip prosthesis from restless movement in bed
Acute kidney injury and organ failure from worsening shock
Deep vein thrombosis in the operative leg, since apixaban is on hold
A surgical site infection from the soaked dressing

rationale.correct: The most immediate risk is the complication of the current problem: ongoing shock leads to organ failure.

perOption.a: Restlessness raises the risk of dislocation, but ongoing bleeding threatens life sooner.
perOption.b: Urine output has fallen to 15 mL/hr as blood pressure drops; without treatment, shock will damage the kidneys and other organs.
perOption.c: DVT is a real risk after hip surgery, but bleeding is the current threat.
perOption.d: Infection develops over days, not within the next hour.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse anticipate for the client at this time? Select all that apply.

options.text: Notify the surgeon about the drain output and vital sign changes
Increase the IV fluid rate and prepare to give blood products as prescribed
Make sure a current type and crossmatch is available
Give the scheduled dose of enoxaparin for DVT prevention
Help the client walk to the chair to improve circulation
Keep the client NPO in case a return to surgery is needed

rationale.correct: Report, restore volume and blood, prepare for surgery, and hold anticoagulants and activity while bleeding continues.

perOption.a: The surgeon must evaluate the bleeding and may return the client to surgery.
perOption.b: Volume and red cells restore perfusion and oxygen delivery.
perOption.c: Blood must be ready for transfusion.
perOption.d: Anticoagulants are held while the client is actively bleeding.
perOption.e: Getting up while in shock may cause fainting and falls.
perOption.f: NPO status prepares for a possible return to the operating room.

questions.stem: The surgeon prescribes 2 units of packed red blood cells. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should be done for the first unit.

items.text: Check the unit with a second nurse at the bedside against the client's identification
Confirm the prescription and that consent for transfusion is signed
Start the transfusion slowly and stay with the client for the first 15 minutes

rationale.correct: Transfusion: prescription and consent, bedside two-person check, baseline vital signs, then start slowly and stay for the first 15 minutes.

perOption.b: Two-person checks at the bedside prevent ABO errors.
perOption.c: Baselines are needed to detect a reaction.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client's acute kidney injury is most likely {{b1}}, worsened by {{b2}}.

options.text: prerenal, from loss of fluid through vomiting and diarrhea
postrenal, from a blockage of urine flow
caused by glomerulonephritis
ibuprofen and lisinopril reducing blood flow to the kidneys
the client's age alone
a high-protein diet

rationale.correct: Dehydration with NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors is a common cause of prerenal AKI; spironolactone adds to hyperkalemia.

perOption.b1:a: Dehydration lowers blood flow to the kidneys, which is a prerenal cause.
perOption.b1:b: Nothing suggests obstruction such as an enlarged prostate or stones.
perOption.b1:c: There is no history of infection, hematuria or edema to suggest glomerular disease.
perOption.b2:a: NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors reduce kidney perfusion, especially in a dehydrated client.
perOption.b2:b: Age is a risk factor, but the medications are a direct, correctable cause.
perOption.b2:c: Nothing suggests dietary protein is involved.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition that poses the most immediate threat to the client, 2 actions the nurse should take to address it, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give IV calcium gluconate as prescribed
Give IV regular insulin with dextrose as prescribed
Give the scheduled spironolactone with breakfast
Offer a banana and orange juice for breakfast
Restrict all IV fluids to protect the kidneys

rationale.correct: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is treated first with IV calcium to protect the heart, then insulin and dextrose to shift potassium into cells, with cardiac monitoring and repeat potassium levels.

perOption.c1: A potassium of 6.8 mEq/L with peaked T waves, a widened QRS and a slow, irregular pulse can lead to cardiac arrest.
perOption.c3: Bicarbonate is low, so this is acidosis.
perOption.c4: The client is dehydrated, not overloaded.
perOption.a1: Calcium stabilizes the heart muscle within minutes.
perOption.a2: Insulin moves potassium into cells; dextrose prevents hypoglycemia.
perOption.a3: Spironolactone keeps potassium in the body and must be held.
perOption.a4: These foods are high in potassium.
perOption.a5: The client needs fluids to restore kidney perfusion.
perOption.p1: Monitoring shows whether the dysrhythmia improves or worsens.
perOption.p2: Repeat levels show whether treatment is working.
perOption.p5: Albumin does not guide hyperkalemia treatment.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the admission prescriptions. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride at 125 mL/hr
Lactated Ringer's with 20 mEq/L potassium chloride
Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as needed for nausea
Acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for knee pain

rationale.correct: Question any potassium-containing fluid or potassium-sparing drug in a client with hyperkalemia and AKI.

perOption.a: Isotonic fluid restores volume and kidney perfusion.
perOption.b: Adding potassium to the IV fluid of a client with a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L is dangerous.
perOption.c: An antiemetic is reasonable for a client who has been vomiting.
perOption.d: Acetaminophen is a safer choice than ibuprofen for this client's kidneys.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Identify an unsafe prescription in hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: The client receives IV regular insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50% dextrose to treat the hyperkalemia. Which assessment is most important for the nurse to perform during the next several hours?

options.text: Checking the fingerstick glucose often, as the protocol directs
Weighing the client twice a shift on the same bed scale at the same time
Testing the urine for ketones each time the client voids
Measuring the abdominal girth at the umbilicus once a shift

rationale.correct: After insulin and dextrose for hyperkalemia, monitor glucose closely: hypoglycemia is a common, delayed complication, especially in kidney injury.

perOption.a: Insulin can cause hypoglycemia for several hours after the dose, especially when the kidneys clear insulin slowly.
perOption.b: Weight is useful for fluid status but does not detect the main risk of this treatment.
perOption.c: Ketones are not a concern with this treatment.
perOption.d: Girth does not relate to insulin and dextrose therapy.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor for hypoglycemia after insulin for hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: On day 2, the nurse reviews the client's progress. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the client's condition is improving or not improving.

rows.text: New crackles in both lung bases and SpO2 91%
Heart rate 78/min and regular, with normal T waves

rationale.correct: Rising urine output, falling potassium and creatinine and a normal rhythm show recovery; new crackles mean the fluids may now be too much.

perOption.r1:c1: Urine output has risen above 30 mL/hr.
perOption.r4:c1: Crackles and lower oxygen saturation suggest fluid overload from IV fluids.
perOption.r5:c1: The rhythm has returned to normal.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

caseStudies.title: Hemorrhage after a total hip replacement

exhibits.title: Orthopedic unit, 1600
exhibits.body: A 71-year-old client returned from surgery at 1100 after a right total hip arthroplasty. History: hypertension and atrial fibrillation; apixaban was stopped 3 days before surgery. At 1600 the client is restless and keeps asking for water. Skin is cool and pale. The surgical drain has put out 450 mL of bright red blood since 1400. The dressing has a 6 cm area of fresh drainage.

exhibits.title: Medical unit, 0800
exhibits.body: A 68-year-old client was admitted last night after 4 days of vomiting and diarrhea. Home medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily and ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for knee pain. The client reports weakness and "my heart feels like it's skipping." Mucous membranes are dry. Urine is dark and scant.
